entry: Collection of health effects caused by [[Ionizing radiation|ionizing radiation]] received in high doses over a short time. Symptoms can begin within an hour and last several months, usually starting with nausea, vomiting and loss of appetite. The condition is generally caused by a total dose above 0.7 Gy (70 rad) from a source outside the body, delivered within minutes. Bone marrow syndrome occurs at 0.7 to 10 Gy, and neurovascular syndrome at doses above 50 Gy. Treatment is generally supportive, with [[Blood transfusion|blood transfusions]] and [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]]. Most cases resulted from the [[Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki|atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki]]. The Chernobyl nuclear power plant disaster, the worst such accident, caused 134 cases and 28 deaths.

English mathematician and writer. Lovelace is chiefly known for her work with [[Charles Babbage]] on his proposed mechanical general-purpose [[Computer|computer]], the analytical engine, which was never built. She was the first to recognize that the machine had applications beyond pure calculation, including manipulating symbols and music. In 1843 she translated an article on the engine by Luigi Menabrea and added seven long explanatory notes. One note described a method of using the machine to calculate Bernoulli numbers, often called the first published [[Computer program|computer program]].

She was the only legitimate child of the poet [[Lord Byron|Lord Byron]] and Anne Isabella Milbanke. Her father separated from her mother a month after Ada was born. She married William King in 1835, and he was created Earl of Lovelace in 1838. Lovelace described her approach as "poetical science". She died young of uterine cancer. Modern analyses have questioned whether her independent contributions were overstated.

First human in the Genesis account of creation. Adam is regarded as the first human aware of God in [[Judaism]], [[Christianity]], Gnosticism, [[Islam]] and the Baháʼí Faith. In Christianity, he sinned in the [[Garden of Eden|Garden of Eden]] by eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, introducing sin and death into the world, and humanity can be redeemed only through the crucifixion of Jesus. In Islam he is *khalifa* (successor) on earth and is forgiven when he repents. In Gnostic cosmologies the body is a prison of Adam's soul.

Polish poet, dramatist and political activist. Regarded as a national poet in Poland, Lithuania and Belarus, Mickiewicz was a principal figure in [[Romanticism|Polish Romanticism]] and is widely considered Poland's greatest poet. His poetic drama *Dziady* (*Forefathers' Eve*) and the national epic *Pan Tadeusz* inspired uprisings against the three imperial powers that had partitioned the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]]. The opening of Lithuania's national anthem paraphrases *Pan Tadeusz*.

Born in the Russian-partitioned territory of the former [[Grand Duchy of Lithuania]], he spent five years in exile in central [[Russian Empire|Russia]]. From 1829 he lived abroad, settling in Rome and then Paris, where he lectured on Slavic literature at the Collège de France until he lost the post over his involvement with religious mysticism. In 1849 he founded the French-language newspaper *La Tribune des Peuples*. He died, probably of [[Cholera|cholera]], in [[Istanbul]] while organizing Polish and Jewish forces to fight Russia in the [[Crimean War]]. His remains were moved to Wawel Cathedral in [[Kraków]].

American comedian and actor. Primarily a comedic leading actor in films, he was a cast member of [[Saturday Night Live]] on [[NBC]] from 1990 to 1995. He starred in a string of Hollywood studio comedies, including *Billy Madison* (1995), *Happy Gilmore* (1996) and *The Wedding Singer* (1998), which cumulatively grossed over $2 billion worldwide. In 2021 he signed a four-movie deal with [[Netflix]] worth over $250 million. His dramatic roles include *Punch-Drunk Love* (2002) and *Uncut Gems* (2019). In 2023 he received the Mark Twain Prize for American Humor.

First man and woman in the Abrahamic creation account. Their story underlies the doctrines of the fall of man and original sin in [[Christianity]], which [[Judaism]] and [[Islam]] do not hold. In the [[Book of Genesis|Book of Genesis]], God fashions [[Adam]] from dust and places him in the [[Garden of Eden|Garden of Eden]], forbidding him to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Eve is created from one of his ribs. After a serpent persuades her to eat the fruit, she gives some to Adam; they gain knowledge and shame, and are expelled from the garden. Neither appears elsewhere in the [[Hebrew Bible|Hebrew scriptures]] except in a single genealogy. In Islam both are equally responsible for their sin. Interpretations range from literal to allegorical readings, and genetic studies are cited against a literal single founding pair. The story has been widely depicted in art and literature.

Chain of natural limestone [[Shoal|shoals]] between [[India]] and [[Sri Lanka]]. Also known as Rama Setu, it is 48 km (30 mi) long and runs from Pamban Island, off the southeastern coast of [[Tamil Nadu]], to Mannar Island, off northwestern Sri Lanka, separating the Gulf of Mannar from the Palk Strait. Geological evidence suggests it was once a land connection between India and Sri Lanka. Much of the sea in the area rarely exceeds 1 metre (3 ft) in depth, making passage by boat difficult. In Hindu tradition, as told in the [[Ramayana]], it is the causeway built by [[Rama]]'s army to reach Lanka.

City (metro pop., 1,816,750), administrative seat of Adana Province in southern [[Turkey]]. It lies on the Seyhan River, 35 km (22 mi) inland from the northeastern shore of the [[Mediterranean Sea]], in the heart of Cilicia, a region of about 6 million people. Its location by a pass in the Taurus Mountains made it important for military campaigns and trade in the classical world, and the fertile Çukurova plain supports extensive cultivation of cotton, grains, vegetables and citrus. Its rulers included the [[Hittites]], Persians, Romans and, later, Islamic [[Caliphate|caliphates]], Crusaders, Mamluks and Ottomans. Adana remains a regional centre for trade, agriculture, healthcare and logistics, and is connected to Tarsus and Mersin by rail.

Genus of medium-to-large deciduous trees known as baobabs. Its eight species are native to [[Africa]], [[Australia]] and Madagascar, and have been introduced elsewhere, including Barbados. A genomic and ecological analysis suggests the genus originated in Madagascar, about 21 million years ago. It belongs to the family [[Malvaceae]]. The generic name honours the French naturalist Michel Adanson, who gave the first detailed botanical description of *Adansonia digitata*. Baobabs are among the longest-lived vascular plants, and their fruit is rich in [[Vitamin C|vitamin C]]. In the early 21st century, baobabs in southern Africa began to die off rapidly and mysteriously; the cause has yet to be determined.

Evolutionary process of [[Natural selection|natural selection]] that fits organisms to their environment. In biology the term has three related meanings: the process itself, the state a population reaches during it, and a heritable trait with a functional role that has evolved by natural selection. Adaptation was discussed from ancient times by philosophers such as [[Aristotle]]. In 18th- and 19th-century natural theology it was taken as evidence for a deity, but [[Charles Darwin|Charles Darwin]] and [[Alfred Russel Wallace|Alfred Russel Wallace]] proposed that natural selection explained it. Adaptation is tied to biological fitness, which governs the rate of evolution. Species may co-adapt, as [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] and pollinating insects do, and features may be co-opted for new uses, as the insulating [[Feather|feathers]] of dinosaurs were for bird flight.

Venomous viper species, *Vipera berus*, widespread across [[Europe]] and as far as [[East Asia]]. It has three recognized subspecies and is the only native venomous snake in [[Great Britain]]. Adders feed on small mammals, [[Bird|birds]], [[Lizard|lizards]] and [[Amphibian|amphibians]]. Like most vipers, the species is ovoviviparous, giving birth to live young. Females breed once every two or three years, and litters of three to 20 are usually born in late summer to early autumn. Adults reach 60 to 90 cm (24 to 35 in). The bite is painful but rarely fatal, and the snake is not aggressive. It is not considered threatened, though it is protected in some countries.

City (pop., 2025: 6,287,000), capital and largest city of [[Ethiopia]]. Menelik II founded it in 1886 after finding nearby Mount Entoto unpleasant, and it became the empire's capital in 1889. Its mineral springs attracted nobles, then artisans, merchants and foreign visitors. Urban development began in the 20th century without prior planning, and later masterplans were drawn up under Italian occupation and by French and British consultants. At an elevation of 2,355 metres (7,726 ft), it is the highest capital in Africa. It is the headquarters of the [[African Union]] and the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, and home to Addis Ababa University. The name is [[Amharic]] for "new flower".

One of the four basic [[Arithmetic|arithmetic]] operations, usually denoted by the plus sign (+). The other three are subtraction, multiplication and division. Adding two whole numbers gives their total, or sum, as in 3 + 2 = 5. Addition is commutative and associative, and adding 0 leaves a number unchanged. It can be defined for abstract [[Integer|integers]], [[Real number|real numbers]] and [[Complex number|complex numbers]], and in algebra for vectors and [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrices]]. Children learn it in primary education, and mechanical aids for it range from the ancient abacus to the modern computer. The plus sign first appeared in a 1456 German manuscript.

Capital (pop., 2024: 1,341,430) and most populous city of [[South Australia]]. Adelaide is the fifth-most populous city in [[Australia]]. Founded in 1836 as a planned settlement for free British migrants, it was laid out on a grid by Colonel William Light, with wide boulevards and public squares. It was named for Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen, wife of King [[William IV]]. Known as the City of Churches for its diversity of faiths, it hosted the first Australian Grand Prix under the [[Formula One]] banner from 1985 to 1995. The city is classed as a Gamma+ level [[Global city|global city]], and its Mediterranean climate supports wine production in the region.

English singer-songwriter. Known for her mezzo-soprano vocals and sentimental songwriting, she has won [[Grammy Awards|16 Grammy Awards]]. Her debut album, *19* (2008), was followed by *21* (2011), which became the best-selling album of the 21st century and topped the Billboard 200 for 24 weeks. In 2013 she won the Academy Award for Best Original Song for "Skyfall", from the [[James Bond]] film. Her albums *25* (2015) and *30* (2021) were the best-selling albums worldwide in their years. Her sales exceed 120 million records worldwide.

Ancient port city (pop., 2026: 1,194,160) on the north coast of the [[Gulf of Aden]], in southern Arabia. It lies near the eastern approach to the [[Red Sea]], and is a gateway between the Red Sea and the Arabian Sea. Under the [[British Empire|British Empire]] from 1839 until 1967, it became a coaling station after the [[Suez Canal]] opened in 1869. Little Aden was the site of an [[Oil refinery|oil refinery]], operated by British Petroleum until South Yemen took control in 1978. Aden was the capital of South Yemen from 1967 until its union with North Yemen in 1990. Since the Houthi takeover of [[Sanaa]] in 2014, it has been the temporary capital of the internationally recognized government of [[Yemen]].

Nucleoside triphosphate that supplies free energy in living cells. ATP provides about 58 kJ/mol (0.6 eV) to drive processes such as [[Muscle contraction|muscle contraction]], nerve impulse propagation and chemical synthesis. It is found in all known forms of life and is often called the "molecular unit of currency" for energy transfer. When consumed, it converts to adenosine diphosphate (ADP) or adenosine monophosphate (AMP), and it is regenerated by processes such as [[Cellular respiration|cellular respiration]]. It is also a precursor to [[DNA]] and [[RNA]]. An average adult recycles about 50 kilograms of ATP daily (about 100 [[Mole (unit)|moles]]). It was first isolated in 1929 by Karl Lohmann.

Non-metallic substance, also called glue, that binds two items together and resists their separation. Adhesives can bind different materials, spread stress across a joint, and offer design flexibility compared with [[Welding|welding]], [[Fastener|mechanical fastenings]] and [[Sewing|sewing]]. Their disadvantages include decreased stability at high temperatures and weakness when bonding large objects over small areas. The earliest known use was about 200,000 years ago, when [[Neanderthal|Neanderthals]] made tar from birch bark to bind stone tools to handles. Glue was not widely used in Europe until AD 1500–1700. Synthetic adhesives developed rapidly from the 20th century, and the global market was valued at approximately USD 73 billion as of 2025.

Thermodynamic process that occurs without transferring [[Heat|heat]] between a system and its surroundings. Energy passes to the surroundings only as work or mass flow, which makes the process central to the [[First law of thermodynamics|first law of thermodynamics]]. Some rapid reactions are treated as adiabatic, such as the adiabatic flame temperature, which assumes combustion loses no heat. In [[Meteorology|meteorology]], rising moist air cools as it expands, and excess vapor is idealized as precipitating instantly in a pseudo-adiabatic process. Dry air rising or sinking cools at about 9.8 °C per km.

German multinational athletic apparel and footwear corporation. It is the largest sportswear manufacturer in Europe and the second largest in the world, after Nike. Adolf Dassler and his brother Rudolf ran a shoe business together from 1924. In 1949 Adolf created Adidas and Rudolf established Puma, its rival. Dassler persuaded [[Jesse Owens|Jesse Owens]] to use his spikes at the 1936 Summer Olympics. The three-stripe mark, bought from a Finnish company in 1952, became the company's identity. The brand is known for its gear at the [[FIFA World Cup|FIFA World Cup]]. Its revenue for 2024 was listed at €23 billion, and the company holds an 8.33% stake in Bayern Munich.

Indian filmmaker and studio executive. He is chairman of Yash Raj Films, the Indian film, media and entertainment conglomerate founded by his father, the director Yash Chopra. The films he has produced make him the highest-grossing Indian film producer of all time. He directed *Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge* (1995), which ran for more than 1,000 weeks at a Mumbai theatre. The Film Division of India honored him with National Awards in 1995, 2004, 2007 and 2015. Chopra has rejected the publicity that came with being the son of Yash Chopra.

Varied tribal groups of the [[Indian subcontinent|Indian subcontinent]]. The term *Adivasi*, a 20th-century construct meaning "ancient inhabitants", is a self-designation used by many communities officially listed as Scheduled Tribes in India and as ethnic minorities in Bangladesh. They constitute about 8.6% of India's population (around 104.2 million, according to the 2011 Census) and about 1.1% of Bangladesh's population (roughly 2 million, 2010 estimate). Many communities formed during or after the [[Indus Valley Civilisation|Indus Valley Civilization]], and carry ancestry from Dravidian, Indo-Aryan, Austroasiatic and Tibeto-Burman peoples. Adivasi studies is a new scholarly field drawing on archaeology, anthropology, and subaltern and indigenous studies.

Part of speech that describes or defines a [[Noun|noun]] or noun phrase. Adjectives change the information given by the noun. In English they are one of the main parts of speech, although words such as *the*, *this* and *my* are now usually classed as determiners. An adjective may precede its noun, as in *a red car*, follow a [[Verb|linking verb]], as in *the car is red*, or stand alone as a substantive, as in *the good, the bad and the funny*. Many adjectives are gradable, taking forms such as *bigger* and *biggest*, while others, such as *dead* and *unique*, are not. In English many adjectives derive [[Adverb|adverbs]], as *quick* gives *quickly*.

Branch of public law governing the activities of [[Executive (government)|executive-branch]] agencies of government. It covers agency rulemaking, which produces regulations, adjudication, and the enforcement of laws. Its areas include international trade, manufacturing, the environment, taxation, broadcasting, immigration and transport. It expanded greatly in the 20th century as [[Legislature|legislative bodies]] created more agencies to regulate economic and social life. Civil law countries often have specialized administrative courts that review decisions. Over the last fifty years, many civil law countries have been influenced by supranational legal orders, and within the [[United Nations]] system, administrative structures have grown in areas such as the environment. Debate continues over the nondelegation doctrine, with critics arguing that transferring legislative power to agencies erodes constitutional separation of powers.

Multimedia software platform for producing animations, rich Internet applications and interactive web content. Originally FutureSplash Animator, it was rebranded by Macromedia as Flash 1.0 in December 1996. [[Adobe Inc.|Adobe]] acquired Macromedia in 2005. Flash powered video, browser games and site navigation in the late 1990s and 2000s. It was a frequent target for exploits, with over 1,000 security vulnerabilities documented since 2005. Adobe announced the end of Flash Player support on December 31, 2020, and content blocking began January 12, 2021. Although Adobe discontinued Flash Player, it is still developed by Zhongcheng for the Chinese market and by Wipro for enterprise customers.
